description: We are The Coalition, a technology-driven team of developers, innovators, and problem-solvers passionate about space exploration and building impactful solutions. Our interests include software engineering, AI/ML, web development, data visualization, and scientific innovation. We aim to turn NASA's open data into practical, interactive solutions. We welcome passionate contributors with expertise in astronomy, astrophysics, mathematics, GIS, research, and UI/UX design.
summary: T-MINUS is a 3D space mission design game in which players build a 3U CubeSat and its rocket part by part, bolt and wire every joint, launch with real physics, and operate the satellite for 30 days. Every choice has a consequence: a loose bolt can fail at max-Q, a wrong cable can cut power, and a bad orbit can miss its target. After each flight, a debrief explains every success and failure, and HOUSTON, the in-game assistant, recommends parts and explains why. Failure Lab jobs recreate real events, such as the Apollo 12 lightning strike and a broken Pathfinder rocket. The physics is real: gravity, air density, drag, the rocket equation and orbital mechanics. The game is built for students aged 12 and up and first-year university students, to show why small engineering decisions decide whether a mission succeeds.
details:
T-MINUS puts the player in charge of a real mission design. Players assemble a 3U CubeSat in the Integration Bay, then build and wire the rocket in the Vehicle Assembly Building. A pre-launch checklist and a GO/NO-GO poll let one to four players, with crew roles, decide whether to launch. The flight runs on a physics model written in C#: a double-precision 2D solver with a fixed 0.05 second RK4 step, air density that falls with altitude, drag that changes with Mach number, staging, and joint failure at max-Q. After orbit insertion, operations run for 30 days, covering power, eclipse, battery charge, imaging and downlink. Every number on screen has a one-line explanation, and every gameplay event goes to an event log that the debrief and HOUSTON read.

What it does: players learn by building, launching and repairing, instead of only reading about spaceflight. The Failure Lab recreates real events, including the Apollo 12 lightning strike and a broken Pathfinder rocket.

Benefits and impact: the game shows that small engineering details, such as a single bolt or cable, decide mission success. It gives teachers a hands-on way to teach orbital mechanics and systems engineering. HOUSTON answers in English or Urdu.

Tools: Unity 6 with URP and UI Toolkit, C#, Newtonsoft JSON, Blender for the 3D parts, and a serverless proxy for the HOUSTON assistant.

Creativity: the build-and-bolt loop borrows from PC-building games, applied to a satellite and rocket.

Factors we considered: accessibility (text size, reduced motion, low-graphics mode), performance on weaker laptops (the Demo Live preset keeps every room at 30 fps or better), and scientific honesty (values that are game choices, not measurements, are labelled as such, and the formulas are tested).
